text: Let me strive on toward the heights and reach the farthest rank.
author: Antara ibn Shaddad
source: Poem 'Da'ni ajidd ila al-'ulya fi al-talab', v. 1

text: Honesty is made of fairness and courage.
author: Ibn Hazm
source: Al-Akhlaq wa al-Siyar fi Mudawat al-Nufus, ch. 'On how people deal with one another in character' (Fasl fima yata'amal bihi al-nas fi al-akhlaq)

text: Resolve comes in the measure of the resolute, and noble deeds in the measure of the noble.
author: Al-Mutanabbi
source: Diwan al-Mutanabbi, qasida 'على قدر أهل العزم تأتي العزائم', opening verse

text: Small deeds look great in small eyes, and great deeds look small in great eyes.
author: Al-Mutanabbi
source: Diwan al-Mutanabbi, qasida 'على قدر أهل العزم تأتي العزائم', verse 2

text: If you venture after a lofty goal, don't settle for anything below the stars.
author: Al-Mutanabbi
source: Diwan al-Mutanabbi, qasida 'إذا غامرت في شرف مروم', opening verse

author: Al-Mutanabbi
source: Diwan al-Mutanabbi, qasida 'الرأي قبل شجاعة الشجعان', verses 1–2

author: Al-Shanfara
source: Lamiyyat al-'Arab, verse beginning 'wa u'dim ahyanan'

author: Ahmed Shawqi
source: Elegy 'Al-Mashriqan 'alayka yantahibān', v. 16 (verse counted by me on the Wikisource text)

author: William Shakespeare

text: Always do what you are afraid to do.

author: Theodore Roosevelt
source: The Strenuous Life (speech of 1899), in The Strenuous Life, 1900

text: I'm not afraid of storms, for I'm learning how to sail my ship.
author: Louisa May Alcott

author: Abraham Lincoln
source: Address at Cooper Institute, New York, 1860

author: Frederick Douglass
source: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave, 1845

author: Robert Browning

author: Booker T. Washington

author: Antonio Machado
source: Campos de Castilla (1912), «Proverbios y cantares», XI

source: Don Quijote de la Mancha, Parte II, cap. LXIII

author: Miguel de Cervantes
source: Don Quijote de la Mancha, Parte II, cap. XLI

author: Spanish proverb
source: Don Quijote de la Mancha, Parte II, cap. X (refrán citado en el texto)

author: Victor Hugo

author: Michel de Montaigne

author: Vauvenargues

author: Virgil

author: Matthias Claudius

author: Adolph Freiherr Knigge
source: Über den Umgang mit Menschen (1788), Erstes Kapitel

author: Maxim Gorky

author: Kozma Prutkov

author: Confucius

author: Du Fu

author: Laozi

author: Mencius

author: Samuel Smiles

author: Louisa May Alcott

author: Joseph Joubert

author: Nicolas Boileau

author: French proverb

author: French proverb

author: French proverb

text: At the working man's house hunger looks in, but dares not enter.
author: Benjamin Franklin
source: The Way to Wealth (Poor Richard Improved, 1758)

text: What you have inherited from your fathers, earn it in order to possess it.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
source: Faust. Der Tragödie erster Teil (1808), Nacht (Faust)

text: Work by day, guests by evening! Hard weeks, glad feasts! Let that be your magic word from now on.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
source: Der Schatzgräber (1797; Ausgabe letzter Hand, Bd. 1, 1827), letzte Strophe

text: Custom, then, is the great guide of human life.
author: David Hume
source: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section V

text: Be strict, punctual, orderly, hardworking and diligent in your calling!
author: Adolph Freiherr Knigge
source: Über den Umgang mit Menschen (1788), Erstes Kapitel

text: As iron rusts without use and water putrefies or freezes in the cold, so the mind without exercise spoils.
author: Leonardo da Vinci
source: Frammenti letterari e filosofici, ed. E. Solmi (1900), Pensieri sulla scienza, XXVI «L'inerzia guasta la sottilità dell'ingegno»

text: One can have no greater and no lesser mastery than mastery over oneself.
author: Leonardo da Vinci
source: Frammenti letterari e filosofici, ed. E. Solmi (1900), Pensieri sulla morale, LII «Sentenze, proverbi e simboli»

text: But do you grasp how much easier it is to dream devoutly than to act well?
author: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing

text: One should not go to bed without being able to say that one has learned something that day.
author: Georg Christoph Lichtenberg

text: We should think more about doing well than about being well; and so we would end up being better off too.
author: Alessandro Manzoni

text: True ease in writing comes from art, not chance, As those move easiest who have learned to dance.
author: Alexander Pope
source: An Essay on Criticism (1711), Part II, ll. 362–363

text: What is to become a master starts practicing early.
author: Friedrich Schiller

text: Work is the adornment of the citizen; blessing is the prize of toil.
author: Friedrich Schiller

text: Wisely and slow; they stumble that run fast.
author: William Shakespeare
source: Romeo and Juliet, Act 2, Scene 3 (Friar Laurence)

text: If the way I have shown to lead here seems very hard, it can nevertheless be found.
author: Baruch Spinoza

text: Whoever could make two ears of corn, or two blades of grass, to grow upon a spot of ground where only one grew before, would deserve better of mankind.
author: Jonathan Swift
source: Gulliver's Travels (1726), Part II (A Voyage to Brobdingnag), Chapter VII

text: A person must work, toil by the sweat of his brow, whoever he is; in this alone lies the meaning and aim of his life, his happiness, his delights.
author: Anton Chekhov

text: Work is the form, the content, the element and the purpose of life — of mine, at least.
author: Ivan Goncharov

text: Nature is not a temple but a workshop, and man is the worker in it.
author: Ivan Turgenev

text: Patience and work will grind down anything.
author: Russian proverb

text: Without effort, you can't even pull a little fish out of a pond.
author: Russian proverb

text: Don't sit around with folded arms, and you won't be bored!
author: Russian proverb

text: Diligence overcomes everything!
author: Kozma Prutkov

text: To learn, and to practise what you have learned again and again: is that not a joy?
author: Confucius

text: Read until you have worn through ten thousand scrolls, and your brush will write as if inspired.
author: Du Fu
source: Twenty-two Rhymes Presented to Vice Director Wei
sourceUrl: https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/奉贈韋左丞丈二十二韻

text: A dyke a thousand zhang long can collapse through an ant hole; a lofty house can burn down from a spark through a crack in the chimney.
author: Han Feizi
source: Han Feizi, ch. 21 «Illustrations of Laozi» (Yu Lao)

text: The hard part of resolve is not overcoming others but overcoming yourself. Hence the saying: “Self-mastery is strength.”
author: Han Feizi
source: Han Feizi, ch. 21 «Illustrations of Laozi» (Yu Lao)

text: Mastering others takes force; mastering yourself is true strength.
author: Laozi

text: People often fail when they are almost done. Be as careful at the end as at the beginning, and nothing will fail.
author: Laozi

text: Even with Li Lou's sharp eyes and Gongshu's skill, without compass and square you cannot draw true circles and squares.
author: Mencius

text: Even the hardiest plant cannot grow if it gets one day of sun and ten days of cold.
author: Mencius

text: A mountain track becomes a road if people keep using it; leave it unused for a while, and weeds choke it.
author: Mencius

text: A good name is not won by shortcuts, nor a reputation built by cleverness: the noble person earns them through their own conduct.
author: Mozi

text: Wood held to the line grows straight; metal on the whetstone grows sharp. Learn widely and examine yourself daily, and your mind will be clear.
author: Xunzi

text: Without adding up single steps, you never travel a thousand li; without small streams, there are no rivers or seas.
author: Xunzi

text: Nothing is more visible than what is hidden, nothing more evident than what is subtle. So the noble person is watchful when alone.
author: The Doctrine of the Mean
source: The Doctrine of the Mean, ch. 1

text: The master of his people is not the fool, but the one who knows how to feign not noticing.
author: Abu Tammam
source: Poem 'Law anna dahran radda raj' jawab', verse beginning 'laysa al-ghabiyyu bi-sayyid'

text: One who rises carries no grudge, and one ruled by temper never reaches the heights.
author: Antara ibn Shaddad
source: Poem 'La yahmil al-hiqd man ta'lu bihi al-rutab', v. 1

text: Your reason and your passion are the rudder and the sails of your seafaring soul.
author: Kahlil Gibran

text: I sought one goal that all people seek alike, and found only one: driving away worry.
author: Ibn Hazm
source: Al-Akhlaq wa al-Siyar fi Mudawat al-Nufus, ch. 'On curing souls and reforming bad character' (Fasl fi mudawat al-nufus)

text: Keeping your temper is a form of courage.
author: Ibn Hazm
source: Al-Akhlaq wa al-Siyar fi Mudawat al-Nufus, ch. 'On how people deal with one another in character' (Fasl fima yata'amal bihi al-nas fi al-akhlaq)

text: Patience is what lightens your tasks; impatience is what piles them up.
author: Ibn al-Muqaffa
source: Al-Adab al-Kabir, part 2 'On dealing with friends' (Fi mu'amalat al-asdiqa')

text: Guard yourself against the surge of anger.
author: Ibn al-Muqaffa
source: Al-Adab al-Kabir, part 2 'On dealing with friends' (Fi mu'amalat al-asdiqa')

text: Patience is of two kinds: patience with what you dislike, and patience in holding back from what you love.
author: Ibn al-Muqaffa
source: Al-Adab al-Kabir, part 2 'On dealing with friends' (Fi mu'amalat al-asdiqa')

text: When I say something false I raise my voice; when I say something certain I speak in a whisper.
author: Abu al-Ala al-Maarri
source: Poem 'Ka-anna munajjim al-aqwam a'ma', last verse

text: What our souls chase is too small to be worth hating and ruining one another over.
author: Al-Mutanabbi
source: Diwan al-Mutanabbi, qasida 'صحب الناس قبلنا ذا الزمانا'

text: Be patient through life's comforts and hardships: the two are equal.
author: Ahmed Shawqi
source: Elegy 'Al-Mashriqan 'alayka yantahibān', v. 26 (verse counted by me on the Wikisource text)

text: Be not disturbed at trifles, or at accidents common or unavoidable.
author: Benjamin Franklin
source: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin (the plan of thirteen virtues), written 1771–1790

text: Calmness of mind is one of the beautiful jewels of wisdom.
author: James Allen

text: Think only of the past as its remembrance gives you pleasure.
author: Jane Austen

text: Where you tend a rose, my lad, A thistle cannot grow.
author: Frances Hodgson Burnett

text: Nature never did betray The heart that loved her.
author: William Wordsworth
source: Lines Written a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey, Lyrical Ballads, 1798

text: Nothing can bring you peace but yourself.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: Be still, sad heart! and cease repining; Behind the clouds is the sun still shining.
author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow

text: Why should we live with such hurry and waste of life?
author: Henry David Thoreau
source: Where I Lived, and What I Lived For, Walden, 1854

text: I needed to be made to feel that there was real, permanent happiness in tranquil contemplation.
author: John Stuart Mill
source: Autobiography, 1873 (chapter on a crisis in his mental history)

text: Serene, I fold my hands and wait, Nor care for wind, or tide, or sea.
author: John Burroughs
source: Waiting, 1862 (text as printed in Famous Single Poems, 1924)

text: I stay my haste, I make delays, For what avails this eager pace?
author: John Burroughs
source: Waiting, 1862 (text as printed in Famous Single Poems, 1924)

text: What is this life if, full of care, We have no time to stand and stare.
author: W. H. Davies
source: Leisure, Songs of Joy and Others, 1911

text: I loafe and invite my soul, I lean and loafe at my ease observing a spear of summer grass.
author: Walt Whitman

text: Time is but the stream I go a-fishing in.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: Let nothing disturb you, let nothing frighten you, all things pass.
author: Teresa of Ávila

text: Let us give time time: for the glass to overflow, it must first be filled.
author: Antonio Machado

text: How restful is the life of one who flees the worldly noise and follows the hidden path taken by the few wise ones the world has known!
author: Fray Luis de León

text: Love your rhythm and set your actions to its law, as you do your verses.
author: Rubén Darío
source: Prosas profanas (1896; ed. 1901), «Las ánforas de Epicuro»

text: A man of great peace is a man of long life.
author: Baltasar Gracián
source: Oráculo manual y arte de prudencia (1647), aforismo 192

text: Fortune is not overcome by injustice and revenge, for they only provoke it further.
author: Pedro Calderón de la Barca
source: La vida es sueño (1635), Jornada tercera

text: Thought consoles us for everything and remedies everything.
author: Chamfort

text: All our trouble comes from not being able to be alone.
author: Jean de La Bruyère

text: The sky above the roof is so blue, so calm!
author: Paul Verlaine

text: Be good, O my Sorrow, and keep more quiet.
author: Charles Baudelaire

text: Patience and length of time do more than strength or rage.
author: Jean de La Fontaine
source: Fables, II, 11, Le Lion et le Rat, 1668

text: When we cannot find peace within ourselves, it is useless to seek it elsewhere.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
source: Réflexions ou sentences et maximes morales, 1678

text: The heart must be at peace, and no passion must come to disturb its calm.
author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau

text: I take people gently as they are; I accustom my soul to bear what they do.
author: Molière

text: Desire burns us and Power destroys us; but Knowledge leaves our frail organism in a perpetual state of calm.
author: Honoré de Balzac

text: My third maxim was always to try to master myself rather than fortune, and to change my desires rather than the order of the world.
author: René Descartes

text: All of humanity's misfortune comes from one thing: not knowing how to stay quietly in a room.
author: Blaise Pascal

text: Time heals sorrows and quarrels, because we change.
author: Blaise Pascal

text: Patience is the art of hoping.
author: Vauvenargues

text: Wisdom is rest in the light.
author: Joseph Joubert

text: Everything comes in good time to those who know how to wait.
author: French proverb

text: Anyone can get angry, and it is easy; but doing it with the right person, to the right degree, at the right time, for the right aim and in the right way is not.
author: Aristotle

text: Never say of anything, “I have lost it,” but rather, “I have given it back.”
author: Epictetus

text: Behave in life as at a banquet: when a dish reaches you, take a modest share; if it hasn't come yet, wait.
author: Epictetus

text: We must make the best of what is in our power, and take the rest as it naturally comes.
author: Epictetus

text: Freedom is won not by satisfying our desires, but by removing them.
author: Epictetus

text: People are disturbed not by things themselves, but by the views they take of those things.
author: Epictetus

text: The future is neither wholly ours nor wholly beyond us: let's not count on it as certain, nor despair of it as lost.
author: Epicurus

text: Not even the greatest wealth can end the soul's turmoil or create joy worth the name.
author: Epicurus

text: One who is untroubled within does not trouble anyone else.
author: Epicurus

text: Do nothing in your life that would make you afraid if your neighbor found out.
author: Epicurus

text: Changing, it finds rest.
author: Heraclitus

text: The best treasure among people is a sparing tongue, and the most grace comes from speech that keeps its measure.
author: Hesiod

text: “Unlucky me, that this happened.” No: lucky me, that even after this happened I remain free from distress.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: Don't let the future trouble you: you'll meet it, if you must, with the same reason you now use for the present.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: A mind free from passions is a fortress.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: Nothing in human affairs is worth great anxiety.
author: Plato

text: Whoever has learned to take things lightly and in moderation becomes the easiest and gentlest person to be with.
author: Plutarch

text: Suffering, long years, and a noble spirit teach me to be content.
author: Sophocles

text: Time is a kindly god.
author: Sophocles

text: Be steady and gentle as the moment demands: the wise adapt their ways to the times without fault.
author: Distichs of Cato

text: Sometimes win over someone you could beat by simply bearing with them: patience is the greatest virtue of character.
author: Distichs of Cato

text: Don't argue about uncertain things when angry: anger keeps the mind from seeing the truth.
author: Distichs of Cato

text: Set some joys among your cares from time to time, and you will bear any labor with a steady mind.
author: Distichs of Cato

text: There is indeed a medicine for the mind: philosophy. And unlike remedies for the body, its help need not be sought from outside.
author: Cicero

text: To be dazzled by nothing, Numicius, is almost the one thing that can make a person happy and keep them so.
author: Horace

text: It is hard; but patience makes lighter whatever cannot be set right.
author: Horace

text: A mind content with the present should not fret about what lies beyond, but soften bitter things with an easy smile: nothing is perfect in every way.
author: Horace

text: There is a measure in all things; there are fixed limits, and what is right cannot stand beyond them or short of them.
author: Horace

text: What we should ask for is a sound mind in a sound body.
author: Juvenal

text: Nothing is sweeter than to dwell in the calm, high sanctuaries of the wise, well fortified by learning.
author: Lucretius

text: Nature asks for nothing more than a body free of pain and a mind that enjoys pleasant feeling, without worry or fear.
author: Lucretius

text: Be willing to be what you are, and wish to be nothing else; neither fear your last day nor long for it.
author: Martial

text: No quarrels, little ceremony, a quiet mind; honest strength, a healthy body; wise simplicity, friends as equals.
author: Martial

text: You will go safest by the middle way.
author: Ovid

text: You will win more surely by reflection than by anger.
author: Publilius Syrus
source: Sententiae, C 11 (entry order in The Latin Library list)

text: The cure for wrongs done to you is to forget them.
author: Publilius Syrus
source: Sententiae, I 21 (entry order in The Latin Library list)

text: All waiting is irksome, but it makes us wise.
author: Publilius Syrus
source: Sententiae, M 3 (entry order in The Latin Library list)

text: A patient mind holds hidden riches.
author: Publilius Syrus
source: Sententiae, P 29 (entry order in The Latin Library list)

text: It is foolish to fear what cannot be avoided.
author: Publilius Syrus
source: Sententiae, S 6 (entry order in The Latin Library list)

text: The greatest remedy for anger is delay.
author: Seneca

text: I believe the most useful thing in life is: nothing in excess.
author: Terence

text: Cheerfulness keeps up a kind of daylight in the mind, and fills it with a steady and perpetual serenity.
author: Joseph Addison

text: The rose has no why; it blooms because it blooms. It does not care for itself, nor ask whether it is seen.
author: Angelus Silesius

text: Stop! Where are you running to? Heaven is within you.
author: Angelus Silesius

text: Certainly, in taking revenge, a man is but even with his enemy; but in passing it over, he is superior.
author: Francis Bacon
source: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral (1625), Of Revenge

text: Fortune is like the market; where many times if you can stay a little, the price will fall.
author: Francis Bacon
source: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral (1625), Of Delays

text: And if they all denounce you, wrap yourself in your own self.
author: Matthias Claudius

text: Come after me, and let people talk: stand like a firm tower whose top never shakes, however the winds may blow.
author: Dante Alighieri

text: Let us forget that there is such a thing as time, and do not count the days of life!
author: Friedrich Hölderlin
source: Hyperion oder Der Eremit in Griechenland (1797/99)

text: We are never as happy or as unhappy as we imagine.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
source: Réflexions ou sentences et maximes morales (1678), maxime 49

text: The moderation of happy people comes from the calm that good fortune gives to their temperament.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
source: Réflexions ou sentences et maximes morales (1678), maxime 17

text: Patience protects against insults just as clothes protect against the cold.
author: Leonardo da Vinci
source: Frammenti letterari e filosofici, ed. E. Solmi (1900), Pensieri sulla morale, XLIX «Comparazione della pazienza»

text: So in this immensity my thought drowns; and sweet to me is shipwreck in this sea.
author: Giacomo Leopardi

text: They also serve who only stand and wait.
author: John Milton
source: Sonnet XIX («When I consider how my light is spent», c. 1655), last line

text: How poor are they that have not patience! What wound did ever heal but by degrees?
author: William Shakespeare

text: An emotion that is a passion ceases to be a passion as soon as we form a clear and distinct idea of it.
author: Baruch Spinoza

text: Accept both praise and slander with indifference, and do not argue with a fool.
author: Alexander Pushkin

text: Then the unrest of my soul subsides, the furrows on my brow smooth out, and I can comprehend happiness on earth…
author: Mikhail Lermontov

text: Only learn to live within yourself! Your soul holds a whole world of mysterious, enchanted thoughts.
author: Fyodor Tyutchev

text: Patience and time — these are my mighty warriors!
author: Leo Tolstoy

text: I don't regret, I don't call, I don't weep; all will pass like smoke from the white apple trees.
author: Sergei Yesenin

text: The slower you go, the farther you'll get.
author: Russian proverb

text: There is no happiness in the world, but there is peace and freedom.
author: Alexander Pushkin

text: I thought: “Pitiful man. What does he want! The sky is clear, beneath it there's room for all, but endlessly and in vain he alone wages war — why?”
author: Mikhail Lermontov

text: The noble person is open and at ease; the petty person is always anxious.
author: Confucius

text: Don't rush, and don't chase small gains. Rush, and you won't arrive; chase small gains, and great things won't get done.
author: Confucius

text: Know where to rest, and you become settled; settled, you grow still; still, you find peace; at peace, you can reflect; reflecting, you attain.
author: The Great Learning
source: The Great Learning, classic text (Zhu Xi arrangement)

text: The highest good is like water. Water benefits all things and does not compete.
author: Laozi

text: Who can make muddy water clear? Through stillness, it slowly becomes clear.
author: Laozi

text: On tiptoe, you cannot stand firm; with overlong strides, you cannot walk far.
author: Laozi

text: The heavy is the root of the light; stillness is the master of restlessness.
author: Laozi

text: Giving up as useless is never weeding your sprouts; forcing growth is pulling the sprouts up, which does not help but harms.
author: Mencius

text: Don't listen to the rain beating through the leaves. Why not chant and whistle, and walk on slowly?
author: Su Shi
source: To the tune Ding Feng Bo

text: How do we know the Way? With the mind. How does the mind know? By being open, unified and still.
author: Xunzi

text: No one seeks their reflection in running water, but in still water. Only what is still can bring stillness to others.
author: Zhuangzi
source: Zhuangzi, ch. 5 «The Sign of Virtue Complete» (De Chong Fu)

text: The perfect person uses the mind like a mirror: it neither chases nor welcomes, it reflects but does not hold on, and so is never hurt.
author: Zhuangzi
source: Zhuangzi, ch. 7 «Fit for Emperors and Kings» (Ying Di Wang)

text: The noble person cultivates the self through calm and nurtures virtue through simplicity.
author: Zhuge Liang
source: Admonition to His Son (Jie Zi Shu)

text: Yesterday is but today's memory and tomorrow is today's dream.
author: Kahlil Gibran

text: Even if study had no other use, it would free you from draining anxieties and empty hopes that bring only worry.
author: Ibn Hazm
source: Al-Akhlaq wa al-Siyar fi Mudawat al-Nufus, ch. 'On knowledge' (Fasl fi al-'ilm)

text: Too many books hold learners back: one lifetime cannot cover everything written on even a single craft.
author: Ibn Khaldun
source: Al-Muqaddima, ch. 6, sec. 34 'Too many books hinder learning'; Wikisource part 6

text: Mastery of a field comes only by building real skill in grasping its principles and rules.
author: Ibn Khaldun
source: Al-Muqaddima, ch. 6, sec. 2 'Teaching a science is a craft'; Wikisource part 5

text: Learn to listen well, just as you learn to speak well.
author: Ibn al-Muqaffa
source: Al-Adab al-Kabir, part 2 'On dealing with friends' (Fi mu'amalat al-asdiqa')

text: Choose the more important of two tasks and keep at it until it is done.
author: Ibn al-Muqaffa
source: Al-Adab al-Kabir, part 2 'On dealing with friends' (Fi mu'amalat al-asdiqa')

text: Make yourself love learning until it becomes your pastime, your pleasure and your comfort.
author: Ibn al-Muqaffa
source: Al-Adab al-Kabir, part 2 'On dealing with friends' (Fi mu'amalat al-asdiqa')

text: Take what you see and let go of what you've merely heard: the rising moon spares you the search for Saturn.
author: Al-Mutanabbi
source: Diwan al-Mutanabbi, qasida 'أجاب دمعي وما الداعي سوى طلل'

text: Whoever spends his hours piling up money for fear of poverty has already done what poverty would do.
author: Al-Mutanabbi
source: Diwan al-Mutanabbi, qasida 'أطاعن خيلا من فوارسها الدهر'

text: What use are a person's eyes if, to him, light and darkness are all the same?
author: Al-Mutanabbi
source: Diwan al-Mutanabbi, qasida 'وا حر قلباه ممن قلبه شبم'

text: Our heartbeats tell us: life is only minutes and seconds.
author: Ahmed Shawqi
source: Elegy 'Al-Mashriqan 'alayka yantahibān', v. 20 (verse counted by me on the Wikisource text)

text: Some run through life toward a goal; others run astray, without reins.
author: Ahmed Shawqi
source: Elegy 'Al-Mashriqan 'alayka yantahibān', v. 15 (verse counted by me on the Wikisource text)

text: Dost thou love life? then do not squander time, for that is the stuff life is made of.
author: Benjamin Franklin
source: The Way to Wealth (Poor Richard Improved), 1758

text: The great thing in this world is not so much where we stand, as in what direction we are moving.
author: Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.

text: All books are divisible into two classes, the books of the hour, and the books of all time.
author: John Ruskin

text: The cost of a thing is the amount of what I will call life which is required to be exchanged for it, immediately or in the long run.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: If you can fill the unforgiving minute With sixty seconds' worth of distance run.
author: Rudyard Kipling

text: Trust no Future, howe'er pleasant! Let the dead Past bury its dead! Act,—act in the living Present!
author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow

text: Ask yourself whether you are happy, and you cease to be so.
author: John Stuart Mill
source: Autobiography, 1873 (chapter on a crisis in his mental history)

text: My experience is what I agree to attend to.
author: William James

text: Know the true value of time; snatch, seize, and enjoy every moment of it.
author: Lord Chesterfield

text: He who cherishes a beautiful vision, a lofty ideal in his heart, will one day realize it.
author: James Allen
source: Visions and Ideals, As a Man Thinketh, 1903

text: Happiness, knowledge, not in another place but this place, not for another hour but this hour.
author: Walt Whitman

text: There are pointless occupations, moths of precious time, and it is worse to busy oneself with trifles than to do nothing.
author: Baltasar Gracián
source: Oráculo manual y arte de prudencia (1647), aforismo 33

text: Try not to lose either your time or your sense of shame.
author: José Hernández
source: La vuelta de Martín Fierro (1879), canto XXXII

text: Slow and careful: doing things well matters more than getting them done.
author: Antonio Machado

text: For the prepared, there are no accidents.
author: Baltasar Gracián
source: Oráculo manual y arte de prudencia (1647), aforismo 151

text: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
author: Spanish proverb
source: Don Quijote de la Mancha, Parte I, cap. XXXI (refrán citado en el texto)

text: We must cultivate our garden.
author: Voltaire

text: Let us strive, then, to think well: that is the principle of morality.
author: Blaise Pascal

text: One is not born for glory if one does not know the value of time.
author: Vauvenargues

text: In the fields of observation, chance favors only the prepared mind.
author: Louis Pasteur

text: It is not enough to have a good mind; the main thing is to apply it well.
author: René Descartes

text: What is well conceived is clearly expressed, and the words to say it come easily.
author: Nicolas Boileau

text: True eloquence consists in saying all that is needed, and only what is needed.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
source: Réflexions ou sentences et maximes morales, 1678, maxime 250

text: One must always say what one sees. Above all, one must always — and this is harder — see what one sees.
author: Charles Péguy

text: The scientist does not study nature because it is useful; he studies it because he delights in it, and he delights in it because it is beautiful.
author: Henri Poincaré

text: I have made this letter longer only because I have not had the time to make it shorter.
author: Blaise Pascal

text: A quick mind is no great advantage if it is not also accurate: the perfection of a clock lies not in going fast, but in keeping time.
author: Vauvenargues

text: An educated person seeks precision in each subject only as far as the nature of the subject allows.
author: Aristotle

text: In every task, consider what leads up to it and what follows from it, and then take it on.
author: Epictetus

text: Let silence be the rule, or say only what is necessary, and in few words.
author: Epictetus

text: First tell yourself who you want to be; then do what you have to do.
author: Epictetus

text: Let us not make random guesses about the most important things.
author: Heraclitus

text: We must not act and speak like people asleep.
author: Heraclitus

author: Hesiod

text: Your mind becomes like the thoughts you often dwell on, for the soul is dyed by its thoughts.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: How much time you gain by not watching what your neighbor says, does, or thinks!
author: Marcus Aurelius

author: Marcus Aurelius

text: Know the right moment.

author: Horace

author: Sallust

author: Seneca

author: Seneca

author: Seneca

text: The one who is everywhere is nowhere.
author: Seneca

author: Virgil

author: Francis Bacon
source: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral (1625), Of Youth and Age

author: Francis Bacon
source: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral (1625), Of Studies

author: Robert Burns

author: Matthias Claudius

text: Remember that this day will never dawn again!
author: Dante Alighieri

text: Divide each of the difficulties I examined into as many parts as possible, and as required to resolve them best.
author: René Descartes

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
source: Faust. Der Tragödie erster Teil (1808), Studierzimmer (Mephistopheles)

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
source: Wilhelm Meisters Wanderjahre (1829), Betrachtungen im Sinne der Wanderer

author: Leonardo da Vinci
source: Frammenti letterari e filosofici, ed. E. Solmi (1900), Pensieri sulla morale, XXXIX «L'attimo è fuggevole»

text: Just as eating without appetite harms health, so study without desire spoils the memory, which keeps nothing it takes in.

text: Life flees and does not stop for an hour.
author: Francesco Petrarca

author: Alexander Pope
source: An Essay on Criticism (1711), Part II, ll. 215–216

author: Russian proverb

author: Laozi

author: Mencius

author: Xunzi

author: Zhuangzi

author: Zhu Xi

author: Kahlil Gibran

author: Ibn Hazm

author: Ibn Khaldun

author: Ibn Rushd (Averroes)
source: Fasl al-Maqal fi ma bayna al-Hikma wa al-Shari'a min al-Ittisal (Decisive Treatise)

author: Al-Mutanabbi

author: Al-Mutanabbi

author: Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma

author: Samuel Johnson

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

author: Thomas Carlyle

author: George Eliot

author: Lord Chesterfield

source: Of Studies, The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, 1625

author: Charles Dickens

author: William Shakespeare
source: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare

source: The Way to Wealth (Poor Richard Improved), 1758

author: Baltasar Gracián
source: Oráculo manual y arte de prudencia (1647), aforismo 15

author: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz

author: Benito Pérez Galdós
source: Fortunata y Jacinta (1887), Parte primera, cap. I

author: Baltasar Gracián
source: Oráculo manual y arte de prudencia (1647), aforismo 87

author: Miguel de Cervantes
source: Don Quijote de la Mancha, Parte II, cap. X

author: Vauvenargues

author: Stendhal

author: François Rabelais

author: Michel de Montaigne

text: It takes greater virtues to bear good fortune than bad.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
source: Réflexions ou sentences et maximes morales, 1678, maxime 25

author: François de La Rochefoucauld
source: Réflexions ou sentences et maximes morales, 1678, maxime 168

author: Heraclitus

author: Heraclitus

author: Heraclitus

author: Heraclitus

author: Hesiod

author: Isocrates

author: Plato

author: Plato

author: Socrates

author: Socrates

author: Horace

author: Horace

author: Martial

author: Ovid

author: Ovid

author: Ovid

author: Plautus

author: Pliny the Younger

author: Publilius Syrus

author: Publilius Syrus

author: Sallust

text: What is wisdom? Always wanting the same things and always refusing the same things.
author: Seneca

author: Seneca

author: Seneca

author: Seneca

author: Tacitus

author: Tacitus

text: Happy is the one who has come to know the causes of things.
author: Virgil

text: If the fool would persist in his folly he would become wise.
author: William Blake
source: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell (c. 1790), Proverbs of Hell

text: O wad some Power the giftie gie us To see oursels as ithers see us!
author: Robert Burns

text: Times change, wills change; being changes, confidence changes: the whole world is made of change, always taking on new qualities.
author: Luís de Camões
source: Rimas, soneto «Mudão-se os tempos, mudão-se as vontades» (Obras completas, ed. 1843, vol. II)

text: Consider your origin: you were not made to live like brutes, but to pursue virtue and knowledge.
author: Dante Alighieri

text: For having understood without retaining it does not make knowledge.
author: Dante Alighieri

text: I think, therefore I am.
author: René Descartes

text: Good sense is the best-shared thing in the world.
author: René Descartes

text: Philosophy is written in this grand book that stands continually open before our eyes: I mean the universe.
author: Galileo Galilei

text: All theory, dear friend, is gray, and green the golden tree of life.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
source: Faust. Der Tragödie erster Teil (1808), Studierzimmer (Mephistopheles)

text: Be a philosopher; but, amidst all your philosophy, be still a man.
author: David Hume
source: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section I

text: Language most shows a man: speak, that I may see thee.
author: Ben Jonson

author: Heinrich von Kleist

text: Judge people not by what they say, but by what they do.
author: Adolph Freiherr Knigge
source: Über den Umgang mit Menschen (1788), Erstes Kapitel

text: Do not learn yourself too much by heart; gather new ideas from books and from people.
author: Adolph Freiherr Knigge

text: A person's merit should be judged not by their great qualities, but by the use they know how to make of them.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
source: Réflexions ou sentences et maximes morales (1678), maxime 437

text: Wisdom is the daughter of experience.
author: Leonardo da Vinci
source: Frammenti letterari e filosofici, ed. E. Solmi (1900), Pensieri sulla scienza, XLV «La esperienza»

text: Whoever thinks little errs much.
author: Leonardo da Vinci

text: The sincere effort a person has made to get to the truth is what gives them their worth.
author: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing
source: Eine Duplik (1778); Text bei Projekt Gutenberg-DE unter dem Titel «Über die Wahrheit»

text: Doubt everything at least once, even the proposition that twice two is four.
author: Georg Christoph Lichtenberg

text: It is almost impossible to carry the torch of truth through a crowd without singeing someone's beard.
author: Georg Christoph Lichtenberg

text: The best artist has no concept that a single block of marble does not already contain within its excess.
author: Michelangelo Buonarroti

text: A good book is the precious life-blood of a master spirit, embalmed and treasured up on purpose to a life beyond life.
author: John Milton

text: Apprentice years in the truest sense are the apprenticeship in the art of living.
author: Novalis

text: Trust not yourself, but your defects to know, Make use of every friend—and every foe.
author: Alexander Pope
source: An Essay on Criticism (1711), Part II, ll. 213–214

text: Life is serious; art is cheerful.
author: Friedrich Schiller

text: The web of our life is of a mingled yarn, good and ill together.
author: William Shakespeare

text: Happiness is not the reward of virtue, but virtue itself.
author: Baruch Spinoza

author: Alexander Pushkin

text: We cannot foresee how our word will echo, and sympathy is given to us as grace is given.
author: Fyodor Tyutchev

text: Though man is not eternal, what is eternal is human.

author: Sergei Yesenin

author: Leo Tolstoy

text: Instead of counting your gossiping friends, wouldn't it be better, my dear, to take a look at yourself?
author: Ivan Krylov

text: Humanity moves forward, perfecting its powers.
author: Anton Chekhov

text: Habit is given to us from above: it is a substitute for happiness.
author: Alexander Pushkin

author: Confucius

author: Confucius

author: Confucius

author: Confucius

author: Han Feizi

text: Those who know do not talk; those who talk do not know.
author: Laozi

text: To know that you do not know is best; to think you know when you don't is a sickness.
author: Laozi

text: To believe everything in a book is worse than having no book at all.
author: Mencius

text: I cannot see Mount Lu's true face simply because I am standing on the mountain.
author: Su Shi
source: Written on the Wall of Xilin Temple (Ti Xilin Bi)

text: Knowing is the intent of acting; acting is the work of knowing. Knowing is where acting begins; acting is where knowing is completed.
author: Wang Yangming
source: Instructions for Practical Living (Chuanxi Lu), vol. 1, §5

text: Learning must never stop. Blue dye comes from the indigo plant, yet it is bluer than the plant itself.
author: Xunzi

text: When you see goodness, earnestly keep it in yourself; when you see what is not good, soberly examine yourself.
author: Xunzi

text: Study widely, question closely, think carefully, discern clearly, and act wholeheartedly.
author: The Doctrine of the Mean
source: The Doctrine of the Mean, ch. 20

text: Everyone knows the use of the useful, but no one knows the use of the useless.
author: Zhuangzi
source: Zhuangzi, ch. 4 «In the World of Men» (Ren Jian Shi)

text: You can't talk of the sea to a frog in a well: it is bound by its place. You can't talk of ice to a summer insect: it is bound by its season.
author: Zhuangzi

text: How does the pond stay so clear? Because fresh water flows in from its source.
author: Zhu Xi
source: Thoughts on Reading, No. 1 (Guan Shu You Gan)

text: I saw that the sun is loved all the more because it does not shine on us forever.
author: Abu Tammam
source: Poem 'Sarat tastajir al-dam' khawfa nawa ghad', verse beginning 'fa-inni ra'aytu al-shams'

text: And forget not that the earth delights to feel your bare feet and the winds long to play with your hair.
author: Kahlil Gibran

text: To wake at dawn with a winged heart and give thanks for another day of loving.
author: Kahlil Gibran

text: Contentment is a virtue made of generosity and fairness.
author: Ibn Hazm
source: Al-Akhlaq wa al-Siyar fi Mudawat al-Nufus, ch. 'On how people deal with one another in character' (Fasl fima yata'amal bihi al-nas fi al-akhlaq)

text: Thanking those who do you good is a true duty.
author: Ibn Hazm
source: Al-Akhlaq wa al-Siyar fi Mudawat al-Nufus, ch. 'On the soul's longing for praise and lasting fame'

text: True friends are the best thing you can gain in this world.
author: Ibn al-Muqaffa
source: Al-Adab al-Kabir, part 2 'On dealing with friends' (Fi mu'amalat al-asdiqa')

text: True friends are an adornment in good times and a store of strength in hard ones.
author: Ibn al-Muqaffa
source: Al-Adab al-Kabir, part 2 'On dealing with friends' (Fi mu'amalat al-asdiqa')

text: The days are only on loan: gather what good you can from them.
author: Tarafa ibn al-Abd
source: Mu'allaqa of Tarafa, verse beginning 'la-'amruka ma al-ayyam'

text: To me every hour of the light and dark is a miracle.
author: Walt Whitman

text: I'm so glad I live in a world where there are Octobers.
author: L. M. Montgomery

text: It just makes me feel glad to be alive—it's such an interesting world.
author: L. M. Montgomery

text: When you're hunting for the glad things, you sort of forget the other kind.
author: Eleanor H. Porter

text: Most generally there is something about everything that you can be glad about, if you keep hunting long enough to find it.
author: Eleanor H. Porter

text: The test of all happiness is gratitude.
author: G. K. Chesterton

text: Man is more himself, man is more manlike, when joy is the fundamental thing in him, and grief the superficial.
author: G. K. Chesterton

text: A thing of beauty is a joy for ever: Its loveliness increases; it will never Pass into nothingness.
author: John Keats

text: There is no duty we so much underrate as the duty of being happy.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson

text: The world is so full of a number of things, I'm sure we should all be as happy as kings.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
source: Happy Thought, A Child's Garden of Verses, 1885

text: I learned to look more upon the bright side of my condition, and less upon the dark side, and to consider what I enjoyed rather than what I wanted.
author: Daniel Defoe
source: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe, 1719

text: And then my heart with pleasure fills, And dances with the Daffodils.
author: William Wordsworth
source: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud, Poems in Two Volumes, 1807

text: How glorious a greeting the sun gives the mountains!
author: John Muir

text: Every morning was a cheerful invitation to make my life of equal simplicity, and I may say innocence, with Nature herself.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: To make a prairie it takes a clover and one bee.
author: Emily Dickinson

text: I loved, I was loved, the sun caressed my face. Life, you owe me nothing! Life, we are at peace!
author: Amado Nervo

text: We do not know the good we had until we have lost it.
author: Miguel de Cervantes
source: Don Quijote de la Mancha, Parte II, cap. LIV

text: It is the mark of well-born people to be grateful for the benefits they receive.
author: Miguel de Cervantes
source: Don Quijote de la Mancha, Parte I, cap. XXII

text: Gratitude that consists only of wishes is a dead thing, as faith without works is dead.
author: Miguel de Cervantes
source: Don Quijote de la Mancha, Parte I, cap. L

text: To love beauty is to see the light.
author: Victor Hugo

text: Love what you will never see twice.
author: Alfred de Vigny
source: Les Destinées, 1864, La Maison du berger

text: Gather the roses of life starting today.
author: Pierre de Ronsard

text: The most wasted of all days is the one on which we have not laughed.
author: Chamfort

text: A happy memory is perhaps truer on earth than happiness itself.
author: Alfred de Musset

text: We must laugh before we are happy, for fear of dying without having laughed.
author: Jean de La Bruyère

text: The clearest sign of wisdom is constant cheerfulness.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Essais, I, 26, De l'institution des enfants, 1580

author: François Rabelais

author: Joseph Joubert

text: If we only wanted to be happy, it would soon be done; but we want to be happier than others.
author: Montesquieu

author: Victor Hugo

author: Epicurus

author: Epicurus

text: Nothing is enough for someone to whom enough is too little.
author: Epicurus

author: Epicurus

author: Epicurus

author: Heraclitus

author: Heraclitus

text: A gift, though small, is welcome.
author: Homer

author: Marcus Aurelius

author: Marcus Aurelius

author: Pindar

author: Plutarch

author: Plutarch

author: Socrates

author: Sophocles

author: Distichs of Cato

author: Cicero

author: Cicero

author: Horace

author: Martial

author: Publilius Syrus

author: Publilius Syrus
source: Sententiae, B 8 (entry order in The Latin Library list)

author: Seneca

author: Seneca

author: Seneca

author: Virgil

author: Joseph Addison

author: Matthias Claudius

author: Daniel Defoe

author: Benjamin Franklin

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
source: Faust. Der Tragödie erster Teil (1808), Vorspiel auf dem Theater (Lustige Person)

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
source: Erinnerung (Goethe's Werke, Ausgabe letzter Hand, Bd. 1, 1827, S. 67)

text: Nothing is more idle than to inquire after happiness which Nature has kindly placed within our reach.
author: Samuel Johnson
source: Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia (1759), Chapter XXII

text: He was not of an age, but for all time!
author: Ben Jonson
source: To the Memory of My Beloved, the Author Mr. William Shakespeare (First Folio, 1623)

text: The starry heavens above me and the moral law within me.
author: Immanuel Kant

text: Whoever does not value life does not deserve it.
author: Leonardo da Vinci
source: Frammenti letterari e filosofici, ed. E. Solmi (1900), Pensieri sulla morale, LII «Sentenze, proverbi e simboli»

text: Enjoy it, my boy; this is a sweet state, a happy season.
author: Giacomo Leopardi
source: Il sabato del villaggio (1829), in Canti

author: Georg Christoph Lichtenberg

author: Georg Christoph Lichtenberg

author: William Shakespeare

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

author: Afanasy Fet

author: Vladimir Korolenko

author: Konstantin Balmont

author: Alexander Blok

author: Fyodor Tyutchev

author: Afanasy Fet

text: Frost and sunshine — a wonderful day!
author: Alexander Pushkin

text: Long live the sun, and let the darkness vanish!
author: Alexander Pushkin

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

author: Anton Chekhov

text: Happy, happy, irretrievable days of childhood! How can one not love and cherish their memory?
author: Leo Tolstoy

author: Confucius

author: Confucius

author: Du Fu

author: Laozi

author: Laozi

author: Li Bai
source: Sitting Alone by Jingting Mountain (Du Zuo Jingting Shan)

author: Mencius

text: The clear breeze over the river and the bright moon among the hills: we may take them freely, and they never run out.
author: Su Shi
source: First Rhapsody on the Red Cliff (Qian Chibi Fu)

text: Picking chrysanthemums by the eastern fence, I calmly gaze at the southern hills.
author: Tao Yuanming

author: The Doctrine of the Mean
source: The Doctrine of the Mean, ch. 14

author: Zhuangzi
source: Zhuangzi, ch. 1 «Free and Easy Wandering» (Xiaoyao You)

text: Heaven and earth were born together with me, and all things are one with me.
author: Zhuangzi
source: Zhuangzi, ch. 2 «On the Equality of Things» (Qi Wu Lun)

author: Zhu Xi

text: My people will remember me when things turn serious: it is in the dark night that the full moon is missed.
author: Abu Firas al-Hamdani
source: Poem 'Araka 'asiyy al-dam' shimatuka al-sabr', verse beginning 'sayadhkurunī qawmī'

author: Abu Tammam
source: Poem 'Kuffi wa-ghaki fa-innani laki qali', verse beginning 'la tunkiri 'atal al-karim'

text: For the soul walks upon all paths.
author: Kahlil Gibran

text: The soul unfolds itself, like a lotus of countless petals.
author: Kahlil Gibran

text: You are good when you are one with yourself.
author: Kahlil Gibran

author: Kahlil Gibran

text: A great door to good sense and peace of mind: stop worrying about what people say.
author: Ibn Hazm
source: Al-Akhlaq wa al-Siyar fi Mudawat al-Nufus, ch. 'On curing souls and reforming bad character' (Fasl fi mudawat al-nufus)

text: Justice means giving what you owe, and taking what you are owed.
author: Ibn Hazm
source: Al-Akhlaq wa al-Siyar fi Mudawat al-Nufus, ch. 'On character and conduct' (Fasl fi al-akhlaq wa al-siyar)

text: Everyone has some bad instincts; what sets people apart is how they struggle against them.
author: Ibn al-Muqaffa
source: Al-Adab al-Kabir, part 2 'On dealing with friends' (Fi mu'amalat al-asdiqa')

text: If blame of me comes from someone petty, it only bears witness to my worth.
author: Al-Mutanabbi
source: Diwan al-Mutanabbi, qasida 'لك يا منازل في القلوب منازل'

author: Al-Mutanabbi
source: Diwan al-Mutanabbi, qasida 'تذكرت ما بين العذيب وبارق'

author: Al-Mutanabbi
source: Diwan al-Mutanabbi, qasida 'وا حر قلباه ممن قلبه شبم'

text: Glory and high honour are a page whose heading is good character.
author: Ahmed Shawqi
source: Elegy 'Al-Mashriqan 'alayka yantahibān', v. 18 (verse counted by me on the Wikisource text)

text: Whoever does not honour himself will not be honoured.
author: Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma
source: Mu'allaqa of Zuhayr, verse beginning 'wa man yaghtarib'

text: I am the master of my fate: I am the captain of my soul.
author: W. E. Henley

text: This above all: to thine own self be true.
author: William Shakespeare

text: I am larger, better than I thought, I did not know I held so much goodness.
author: Walt Whitman
source: Song of the Open Road, Leaves of Grass, 1891–92 edition

text: I am no bird; and no net ensnares me; I am a free human being with an independent will.
author: Charlotte Brontë

text: I would always rather be happy than dignified.
author: Charlotte Brontë

text: I care for myself. The more solitary, the more friendless, the more unsustained I am, the more I will respect myself.
author: Charlotte Brontë

text: If I am a princess in rags and tatters, I can be a princess inside.
author: Frances Hodgson Burnett

text: Till this moment, I never knew myself.
author: Jane Austen

text: Be true! Be true! Be true! Show freely to the world, if not your worst, yet some trait whereby the worst may be inferred!
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

text: I'm nobody! Who are you? Are you nobody, too? Then there's a pair of us—don't tell!
author: Emily Dickinson

text: I'd rather see you poor men's wives, if you were happy, beloved, contented, than queens on thrones, without self-respect and peace.
author: Louisa May Alcott

text: Whether I shall turn out to be the hero of my own life, or whether that station will be held by anybody else, these pages must show.
author: Charles Dickens

text: Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: To want to be someone else is to want to stop being who one is.
author: Miguel de Unamuno
source: Del sentimiento trágico de la vida (1913), cap. I «El hombre de carne y hueso»

text: Act so that, in your own judgment and in the judgment of others, you deserve eternity; make yourself irreplaceable; do not deserve to die.
author: Miguel de Unamuno
source: Del sentimiento trágico de la vida (1913), cap. XI «El problema práctico»

text: For I see, at the end of my rough road, that I was the architect of my own destiny.
author: Amado Nervo

text: Everyone dreams what they are, though no one understands it.
author: Pedro Calderón de la Barca
source: La vida es sueño (1635), Jornada segunda

text: I want to live with myself, I want to enjoy the good I owe to heaven.
author: Fray Luis de León

text: Freedom, Sancho, is one of the most precious gifts that heaven has given to men.
author: Miguel de Cervantes
source: Don Quijote de la Mancha, Parte II, cap. LVIII

text: Each of us is the child of our own deeds.
author: Miguel de Cervantes
source: Don Quijote de la Mancha, Parte I, cap. IV

text: Not to climb very high, perhaps, but all on my own!
author: Edmond Rostand

text: I am made unlike any of those I have seen; I dare believe I am made unlike anyone who exists.
author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau

text: For a conscious being, to exist is to change, to change is to mature, to mature is to go on creating oneself endlessly.
author: Henri Bergson

text: Better to be alone than in bad company.
author: French proverb

text: You are never better served than by yourself.
author: French proverb

text: My glass is not large, but I drink from my own glass.
author: Alfred de Musset
source: La Coupe et les Lèvres, 1832, Dédicace

text: The greatest thing in the world is to know how to belong to oneself.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Such a person wants not to seem the best, but to be it.
author: Aeschylus

text: A good person should love themselves: by doing fine things they will benefit themselves and help others.
author: Aristotle

author: Aristotle

text: If you ever turn outward, wanting to please someone, know that you have lost your footing.
author: Epictetus

text: Set yourself, now, a character and a pattern, and keep it both when alone and among people.
author: Epictetus

author: Epictetus

text: “I am richer than you, therefore I am better than you”: such reasoning does not hold.
author: Epictetus

author: Epictetus

text: You are the one who knows what you are worth to yourself and at what price you sell yourself.
author: Epictetus

text: Let praise from others come of its own accord; our task is to care for our own healing.
author: Epicurus

text: I searched into myself.
author: Heraclitus

text: You could not find the limits of the soul, though you travel every road; so deep is its measure.
author: Heraclitus

text: A person's character is their destiny.
author: Heraclitus

text: The soul has a principle that increases itself.
author: Heraclitus

text: The gods do not give every gift to everyone: not looks, nor wit, nor eloquence.
author: Homer

text: Love the modest craft you have learned, and find your rest in it.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: There's much where you can't plead “I have no talent.” Show what is wholly yours: sincerity, dignity, endurance.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: Take care not to turn into a Caesar, not to be dyed by the role. Keep yourself simple, good, pure, dignified.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: I often wonder: we each love ourselves more than anyone, yet value our own opinion of ourselves less than others'.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: Don't be ashamed to be helped.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: Become such as you are, having learned it.
author: Pindar

text: I can't yet know myself, as the Delphic inscription bids; it seems absurd to study other things while ignorant of that.
author: Plato

text: Care for nothing of yours before you care to become as good and wise as you can.
author: Plato

text: As a shoe bends to fit the foot and not the reverse, so our dispositions shape our lives to match themselves.
author: Plutarch

text: If I had to choose, I would rather suffer wrong than do it.
author: Socrates

text: Even for a wise person, there is no shame in learning many things and in not being too rigid.
author: Sophocles

text: What is hardest? To know yourself. What is easiest? To give advice to someone else.
author: Thales

text: Never look down on a small body's strength: whoever nature denied force is strong in judgment.
author: Distichs of Cato

text: Stop opposing yourself: whoever is at odds with himself will get along with no one.
author: Distichs of Cato

text: Look at people's lives and habits: even as they blame others, no one lives without fault.
author: Distichs of Cato

text: Care not only for your body but even more for your mind and spirit: like a lamp, they go out unless you keep adding oil.
author: Cicero

text: What suits each of us best is what is most truly our own.
author: Cicero

text: Let each of us know our own talents, and be a sharp judge of our own strengths and weaknesses.
author: Cicero

text: Anyone can make a mistake; only a fool keeps making it.
author: Cicero

text: It is pointless to fight your own nature or to chase what you cannot reach.
author: Cicero

text: You can always go part of the way, even if you cannot go further.
author: Horace

text: Let this be your wall of bronze: a clear conscience, and no guilt to make you turn pale.
author: Horace

text: You rush to remove what hurts your eye; so why, when something gnaws at your mind, do you put off the cure for a year?
author: Horace

text: I'm annoyed whenever good Homer nods off; yet in a long work it is fair for sleep to creep in.
author: Horace

text: No one is born without faults; the best of us is simply the one weighed down by the smallest.
author: Horace

text: The only true nobility is virtue.
author: Juvenal

author: Juvenal

text: Everyone runs away from themselves this way, yet of course cannot escape the self.
author: Lucretius

text: Even when strength falls short, the will deserves praise.
author: Ovid

text: Unless you think for yourself, listening to the wise is in vain.
author: Publilius Syrus

text: Correct a mistake quickly, and you make it smaller.
author: Publilius Syrus
source: Sententiae, P 62 (entry order in The Latin Library list)

author: Sallust

text: Praise in a person what can be neither taken away nor given: what is truly their own.
author: Seneca

text: A good mind is open to everyone; in this, we are all of noble birth.
author: Seneca
