author: Seneca

text: We are looking for a way for the mind to keep an even, steady course, to be kind to itself, and to look gladly on what is its own.
author: Seneca

text: It is your mind you need to change, not your sky.
author: Seneca

text: The form of the mind is lasting, and you can express it not through another's art or material, but through your own character.
author: Tacitus

text: We cannot all do everything.
author: Virgil

text: They can, because they believe they can.
author: Virgil

text: I have always preferred cheerfulness to mirth. The latter I consider as an act, the former as a habit of the mind.
author: Joseph Addison

text: The pith o' sense, an' pride o' worth, Are higher rank than a' that.
author: Robert Burns
source: A Man's a Man for a' That (1795)

text: Strive and win your own worth; plain home-baked bread nourishes best.
author: Matthias Claudius

text: Heed the voice deep within you; it is a person's jewel here on earth.
author: Matthias Claudius

text: If you follow your star, you cannot fail to reach a glorious port.
author: Dante Alighieri

text: Wait no longer for my word or sign: your will is free, upright and whole.
author: Dante Alighieri

text: The chief part of happiness is to be willing to be what you are.
author: Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam
source: Moriae encomium (Praise of Folly, 1511), Folly's speech on Philautia (self-love)

text: Find your joy in yourself, and count it no hardship even if fortune, place and time have conspired against you.
author: Paul Fleming

text: Yet I was, by the endeavour, a better and a happier man than I otherwise should have been if I had not attempted it.
author: Benjamin Franklin
source: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin (written 1771–1790), on his plan of moral perfection

text: How can we come to know ourselves? Never by contemplation, only by action. Try to do your duty, and you will know at once what is in you.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
source: Wilhelm Meisters Wanderjahre (1829), Betrachtungen im Sinne der Wanderer

text: Every day one should hear at least one little song, read one good poem, see one fine painting.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
source: Wilhelm Meisters Lehrjahre (1795/96), Fünftes Buch, 1. Kapitel (Serlo)

text: Nothing perfectly straight can be built from timber as crooked as that from which humans are made.
author: Immanuel Kant
source: Idee zu einer allgemeinen Geschichte in weltbürgerlicher Absicht (1784), Sechster Satz

text: In this world everyone counts for only as much as they make of themselves.
author: Adolph Freiherr Knigge
source: Über den Umgang mit Menschen (1788), Erstes Kapitel, Nr. 1

text: Act well and decently less to please others than so as not to forfeit your own self-respect!
author: Adolph Freiherr Knigge
source: Über den Umgang mit Menschen (1788), Zweites Kapitel («Über den Umgang mit sich selbst»)

text: At no step of yours should your heart be able to reproach you for your intention or your means.
author: Adolph Freiherr Knigge
source: Über den Umgang mit Menschen (1788), Erstes Kapitel

text: To brood anxiously over what one could have done is the worst thing one can do.
author: Georg Christoph Lichtenberg

text: Nothing is harder than being patient with oneself, than bearing one's own weakness.
author: Novalis

text: To err is human, to forgive, divine.
author: Alexander Pope
source: An Essay on Criticism (1711), Part II, l. 525

text: Dare to err and to dream: deep meaning often lies in childlike play.
author: Friedrich Schiller

text: Self-love, my liege, is not so vile a sin As self-neglecting.
author: William Shakespeare

text: We know what we are, but know not what we may be.
author: William Shakespeare

text: Joy is not directly bad, but good.
author: Baruch Spinoza

text: Everything in a person should be beautiful: the face, the clothes, the soul and the thoughts.
author: Anton Chekhov

text: I like that I can be ridiculous, uninhibited, and not play with words, and not blush in a stifling wave when our sleeves barely touch.
author: Marina Tsvetaeva
source: «Мне нравится, что Вы больны не мной», 1915

text: If the stars are lit, does that mean someone needs it?
author: Vladimir Mayakovsky

text: My gift is meager and my voice is not loud, but I am alive, and on this earth my being is dear to someone.
author: Yevgeny Baratynsky
source: «Мой дар убог и голос мой не громок», 1828

text: Have a heart, have a soul, and you will be a true human being at all times.
author: Denis Fonvizin

text: I'd gladly serve, but being servile makes me sick.
author: Alexander Griboyedov

text: You are a king: live alone. Walk the free road wherever your free mind leads you.
author: Alexander Pushkin

text: To answer to no one, to serve and please only oneself.
author: Alexander Pushkin

text: If you want to be happy, be happy.
author: Kozma Prutkov

text: Unrecognized by others, yet free of bitterness: is that not true nobility?
author: Confucius

text: When you make a mistake, do not be afraid to correct it.
author: Confucius

text: Don't worry about lacking a position; worry about being fit for one. Don't worry about being unknown; strive to be worth knowing.
author: Confucius

text: The noble person looks to themselves; the petty person looks to others.
author: Confucius

text: Making your intentions sincere means not deceiving yourself.
author: The Great Learning
source: The Great Learning, commentary ch. 6 (Zhu Xi arrangement)

text: Knowing others is intelligence; knowing yourself is true clarity.
author: Laozi

text: The greatest vessel is the last to be completed.
author: Laozi

text: Your name or your self: which is dearer? Your self or your wealth: which matters more?
author: Laozi

text: Heaven gave me my talents, so surely they have a use; spend a thousand in gold, and it will all come back.
author: Li Bai
source: Bring in the Wine (Qiang Jin Jiu)

text: A great person is one who has not lost the heart of a newborn child.
author: Mencius

text: People often make mistakes, and only then are they able to change.
author: Mencius

text: All things are complete within me. To look within and find myself true: there is no greater joy.
author: Mencius

text: In hard times, make yourself good; in good times, make the whole world better.
author: Mencius

text: Everyone has a sage within. It's only that they don't trust themselves enough, and so they bury it.
author: Wang Yangming
source: Instructions for Practical Living (Chuanxi Lu), vol. 3, §207

text: Even the greatest sages make mistakes. What still makes them great in the end is that they can correct them.
author: Wang Yangming
source: Instructions for the Students at Longchang (Jiaotiao Shi Longchang Zhusheng)

text: Those who know themselves do not blame others; those who understand fate do not blame Heaven.
author: Xunzi
source: Xunzi, ch. 4 «Of Honour and Disgrace» (Rong Ru)

text: Were the whole world to praise him, he would not be spurred on; were the whole world to condemn him, he would not lose heart.
author: Zhuangzi
source: Zhuangzi, ch. 1 «Free and Easy Wandering» (Xiaoyao You)

text: A duck's legs are short, but stretching them would make it miserable; a crane's legs are long, but cutting them would cause it grief.
author: Zhuangzi

text: If you blame your friend for everything, you will never find one you don't blame.
author: Bashshar ibn Burd
source: Poem 'Jafa wuddahu fa-azwarra aw malla sahibuh'

text: If you won't drink water with a speck in it, you will stay thirsty; whose waters are ever perfectly clear?
author: Bashshar ibn Burd
source: Poem 'Jafa wuddahu fa-azwarra aw malla sahibuh'

text: Let there be spaces in your togetherness.
author: Kahlil Gibran

text: You give but little when you give of your possessions. It is when you give of yourself that you truly give.
author: Kahlil Gibran

text: And let your best be for your friend.
author: Kahlil Gibran

text: Give advice without demanding it be taken, help without demanding success, and give without demanding a return.
author: Ibn Hazm
source: Al-Akhlaq wa al-Siyar fi Mudawat al-Nufus, ch. 'On brothers, friendship and advice' (Fasl fi al-ikhwan wa al-sadaqa wa al-nasiha)

text: Friendship means this: what grieves the other grieves you, and what gladdens the other gladdens you.
author: Ibn Hazm
source: Al-Akhlaq wa al-Siyar fi Mudawat al-Nufus, ch. 'On brothers, friendship and advice' (Fasl fi al-ikhwan wa al-sadaqa wa al-nasiha)

text: Don't carry to your friend news that will hurt him and do him no good to know.
author: Ibn Hazm
source: Al-Akhlaq wa al-Siyar fi Mudawat al-Nufus, ch. 'On brothers, friendship and advice' (Fasl fi al-ikhwan wa al-sadaqa wa al-nasiha)

text: When you give advice, give it in private, not in public, and by gentle hint rather than bluntly.
author: Ibn Hazm
source: Al-Akhlaq wa al-Siyar fi Mudawat al-Nufus, ch. 'On brothers, friendship and advice' (Fasl fi al-ikhwan wa al-sadaqa wa al-nasiha)

text: Among family and neighbours, the one who does not repay wrong with wrong is the noblest of them all.
author: Ibn Hazm
source: Al-Akhlaq wa al-Siyar fi Mudawat al-Nufus, ch. 'On curing souls and reforming bad character' (Fasl fi mudawat al-nufus)

text: Raised by harshness and force, a person finds his spirit cramped, his energy gone and his mind drawn toward idleness.
author: Ibn Khaldun
source: Al-Muqaddima, ch. 6, sec. 40 'Harshness toward learners harms them'; Wikisource part 6

text: Give your friend your life and wealth, acquaintances your help, everyone your smile and warmth, and even your enemy your fairness.
author: Ibn al-Muqaffa
source: Al-Adab al-Kabir, part 2 'On dealing with friends' (Fi mu'amalat al-asdiqa')

text: Never insult or condemn a whole people or nation.
author: Ibn al-Muqaffa
source: Al-Adab al-Kabir, part 2 'On dealing with friends' (Fi mu'amalat al-asdiqa')

text: When someone apologizes to you, meet them with a bright face, a smile and kind words.
author: Ibn al-Muqaffa
source: Al-Adab al-Kabir, part 2 'On dealing with friends' (Fi mu'amalat al-asdiqa')

text: Listening well means letting the speaker finish what they are saying.
author: Ibn al-Muqaffa
source: Al-Adab al-Kabir, part 2 'On dealing with friends' (Fi mu'amalat al-asdiqa')

text: Don't dress yourself in others' words: be content to gather what is right when you hear it and credit its owner.
author: Ibn al-Muqaffa
source: Al-Adab al-Kabir, part 2 'On dealing with friends' (Fi mu'amalat al-asdiqa')

text: No craft can be created by one person alone. How much less the craft of crafts, wisdom?
author: Ibn Rushd (Averroes)
source: Fasl al-Maqal fi ma bayna al-Hikma wa al-Shari'a min al-Ittisal (Decisive Treatise)

text: Don't look down on children at play: they may well grow into leaders of their people.
author: Abu al-Ala al-Maarri
source: Poem 'La tazdarunna sighar fi mala'ibihim', v. 1

text: You have no horses or wealth to give? Then let your words bring joy where your means cannot.
author: Al-Mutanabbi
source: Diwan al-Mutanabbi, qasida 'لا خيل عندك تهديها ولا مال', opening verse

text: Whoever shields his honour with generosity keeps it intact.
author: Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma
source: Mu'allaqa of Zuhayr, verse beginning 'wa man yaj'al al-ma'ruf'

text: The world is a looking-glass, and gives back to every man the reflection of his own face.
author: William Makepeace Thackeray

text: This communicating of a man's self to his friend, works two contrary effects; for it redoubleth joys, and cutteth griefs in halves.
author: Francis Bacon
source: Of Friendship, The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, 1625

text: If I can stop one heart from breaking, I shall not live in vain.
author: Emily Dickinson

text: With malice toward none; with charity for all.
author: Abraham Lincoln

text: The better part of one's life consists of his friendships.
author: Abraham Lincoln

text: What do we live for, if it is not to make life less difficult to each other?
author: George Eliot

text: 'Tis better to have loved and lost Than never to have loved at all.
author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson

text: I love thee with the breath, Smiles, tears, of all my life!
author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning

text: If thou must love me, let it be for nought Except for love's sake only.
author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning

text: His little, nameless, unremembered acts Of kindness and of love.
author: William Wordsworth
source: Lines Written a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey, Lyrical Ballads, 1798

text: No man is an island, entire of itself; every man is a piece of the continent, a part of the main.
author: John Donne
source: Devotions upon Emergent Occasions, Meditation XVII, 1624

text: Write me as one that loves his fellow-men.
author: Leigh Hunt
source: Abou Ben Adhem, 1838 (text as printed in Poems That Every Child Should Know, 1904)

text: Let brothers be united, for that is the first law.
author: José Hernández
source: La vuelta de Martín Fierro (1879), canto XXXII

text: I grow a white rose, in July as in January, for the true friend who gives me his honest hand.
author: José Martí

text: With the poor of the earth I want to cast my lot.
author: José Martí

text: Tell me who you walk with, and I'll tell you who you are.
author: Spanish proverb
source: Don Quijote de la Mancha, Parte II, cap. X (refrán citado en el texto)

text: Great friends are for great occasions.
author: Baltasar Gracián
source: Oráculo manual y arte de prudencia (1647), aforismo 171

text: You say nothing is created? Never mind; with the clay of the earth, make a cup for your brother to drink from.
author: Antonio Machado
source: Campos de Castilla (1912), «Proverbios y cantares», XXXVII

text: I always direct my intentions toward good ends, which are to do good to all and harm to none.
author: Miguel de Cervantes
source: Don Quijote de la Mancha, Parte II, cap. XXXII

text: All for one, one for all.
author: Alexandre Dumas

text: To understand everything makes one very forgiving.
author: Madame de Staël

text: Let us be friends, Cinna; it is I who invite you to it.
author: Pierre Corneille

text: Nothing compares to the pleasures of friendship.
author: Honoré de Balzac

text: Time, which strengthens friendships, weakens love.
author: Jean de La Bruyère

text: Perhaps one must have felt love to truly know friendship.
author: Chamfort

text: It is more shameful to distrust our friends than to be deceived by them.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
source: Réflexions ou sentences et maximes morales, 1678, maxime 84

text: Quarrels would not last long if the fault were only on one side.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
source: Réflexions ou sentences et maximes morales, 1678, maxime 496

text: One cannot go far in friendship unless one is willing to forgive each other's small faults.
author: Jean de La Bruyère

text: The most delicate pleasure is to give pleasure to others.
author: Jean de La Bruyère

text: We often need someone smaller than ourselves.
author: Jean de La Fontaine
source: Fables, II, 11, Le Lion et le Rat, 1668

text: Gentleness achieves more than violence.
author: Jean de La Fontaine

text: What a sweet thing a true friend is!
author: Jean de La Fontaine

text: There are neither weeds nor bad men. There are only bad growers.
author: Victor Hugo

text: Whatever multiplies the bonds that tie man to man makes him better and happier.
author: Joseph Joubert

text: Politeness is to kindness what words are to thought.
author: Joseph Joubert

text: If pressed to say why I loved him, I feel it can only be expressed by answering: Because it was he, because it was I.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: It is easy, when your foot is clear of trouble, to advise and admonish someone who is faring badly.
author: Aeschylus

text: Without friends no one would choose to live, even with all other goods.
author: Aristotle

text: The wish for friendship comes quickly; friendship does not.
author: Aristotle

text: People cannot know each other until they have shared the proverbial salt together.
author: Aristotle

text: A friend is another self.
author: Aristotle

text: Everything has two handles. If your brother wrongs you, don't lift it by the wrong, but by this: he is your brother.
author: Epictetus

text: We don't need our friends' help so much as the confidence that they will help us.
author: Epicurus

text: Friendship dances around the world, calling on each of us to wake up to happiness.
author: Epicurus

text: Let us share our friends' troubles not by lamenting, but by caring for them.
author: Epicurus

text: In troubles, good friends are the clearest to see.
author: Euripides

text: Whoever wants to possess wealth or power rather than good friends is badly mistaken.
author: Euripides

text: A bad neighbor is a plague, a good one a great blessing; whoever has a good neighbor has a share of honor.
author: Hesiod

text: Nothing is better or finer than when a husband and wife keep house together in harmony of mind.
author: Homer

text: When two go together, one sees before the other what will be of use; alone, even a thinker has a narrower mind and thinner counsel.
author: Homer

text: Having done good, a person doesn't dwell on it but moves on to the next, as a vine bears grapes again in season.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: The best revenge is not to become like the one who wronged you.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: Kindness is invincible, if it is genuine and not a forced smile or a pretense.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: I would rather have a good friend than the finest quail in the world, or even all the gold of Darius.
author: Socrates

text: It is my nature to share love, not hate.
author: Sophocles

text: To help others with what one has and can do is the finest of labors.
author: Sophocles

text: We have two ears and one mouth so that we may listen more and speak less.
author: Zeno of Citium

text: The most sacred kind of friend is counted not by fortune, but by virtue.
author: Boethius

text: Can we count on friends whom fortune, not virtue, has brought to us?
author: Boethius

text: Anger breeds hatred; harmony nourishes love.
author: Distichs of Cato

text: If you can, remember to help even strangers: winning friends by kindness is worth more than a kingdom.
author: Distichs of Cato

text: Of all the gifts of friendship, the greatest is this: it lights up hope for the future and does not let our spirits weaken or fall.
author: Cicero

text: Whoever looks at a true friend sees, as it were, an image of himself.
author: Cicero

text: Let this be the first law of friendship: ask friends only for what is right, do what is right for them, and don't wait to be asked.
author: Cicero

text: Those who take friendship out of life seem to take the sun out of the world.
author: Cicero

text: The greatest respect is owed to a child.
author: Juvenal

text: To be loved, be lovable.
author: Ovid

text: To help one another is the best thing a human can do, and it is the road to lasting glory.
author: Pliny the Elder

text: After a quarrel, harmony becomes dearer.
author: Publilius Syrus
source: Sententiae, D 9 (entry order in The Latin Library list)

text: Whoever helps someone in need quickly gives twice.
author: Publilius Syrus
source: Sententiae, I 6 (entry order in The Latin Library list)

text: Whoever gives way to their loved ones is not defeated, but wins.
author: Publilius Syrus
source: Sententiae, N 40 (entry order in The Latin Library list)

text: Through harmony small things grow; through discord even the greatest fall apart.
author: Sallust

text: Once a friendship is formed, trust; before it is formed, judge.
author: Seneca

text: The first thing philosophy promises is fellow-feeling, humanity, and the wish to live together.
author: Seneca

text: No good thing is a joy to own without someone to share it with.
author: Seneca

text: Spend time with those who will make you better; welcome those you can make better. It works both ways: we learn while we teach.
author: Seneca

text: Treat those below you as you would want those above you to treat you.
author: Seneca

text: You must live for someone else if you want to live for yourself.
author: Seneca

text: A human being is something sacred to another human being.
author: Seneca

text: While we draw breath, while we are among people, let us cherish our humanity.
author: Seneca

text: I am a human being; nothing human is foreign to me.
author: Terence

text: So many people, so many opinions: everyone has their own way.
author: Terence

text: Having known hardship myself, I am learning to help those who suffer.
author: Virgil

text: Love conquers all; let us, too, yield to love.
author: Virgil

text: There are tears for what happens, and human troubles touch the heart.
author: Virgil

text: It is human to have compassion for the afflicted.
author: Giovanni Boccaccio

text: That Man to Man, the world o'er, Shall brothers be for a' that.
author: Robert Burns
source: A Man's a Man for a' That (1795)

text: A noble heart shines bright and kind; a good one is pure gold.
author: Matthias Claudius

text: For love, all love of other sights controls, And makes one little room an everywhere.
author: John Donne

text: If we treat people as if they were what they ought to be, we bring them to where they can be brought.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
source: Wilhelm Meisters Lehrjahre (1795/96), Achtes Buch, 4. Kapitel (Natalie, im Brief Thereses)

text: Let man be noble, helpful and good!
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
source: Das Göttliche (entstanden 1783, Erstdruck 1789 in Goethes Schriften, Bd. 8), 1. Strophe

text: No man is so foolish but may give another good counsel sometimes; and no man is so wise but may easily err, if he will take no others' counsel but his own.
author: Ben Jonson

text: Take an interest in others if you want others to take an interest in you!
author: Adolph Freiherr Knigge
source: Über den Umgang mit Menschen (1788), Erstes Kapitel, Nr. 13

text: Do not seek to make anyone ridiculous in company, not even the weakest.
author: Adolph Freiherr Knigge
source: Über den Umgang mit Menschen (1788), Erstes Kapitel

text: Nothing is so contagious as example, and we never do great good or great evil that does not produce its like.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
source: Réflexions ou sentences et maximes morales (1678), maxime 230

text: The pleasure of love is to love.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
source: Réflexions ou sentences et maximes morales (1678), maxime 259

text: We forgive for as long as we love.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
source: Réflexions ou sentences et maximes morales (1678), maxime 330

text: For truly, great love is born of great knowledge of what one loves.
author: Leonardo da Vinci
source: Frammenti letterari e filosofici, ed. E. Solmi (1900), Pensieri sulla morale, XLIII

text: Come, we must, we must be friends!
author: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing

text: I have never demanded that all trees grow the same bark.
author: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing

text: Let each strive after his incorruptible love, free of prejudice!
author: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing

text: Before you criticize, always try first whether you cannot excuse.
author: Georg Christoph Lichtenberg

text: Good-nature and good sense must ever join.
author: Alexander Pope
source: An Essay on Criticism (1711), Part II, l. 524

text: The honest man thinks of himself last.
author: Friedrich Schiller

text: Love all, trust a few, Do wrong to none.
author: William Shakespeare
source: All's Well That Ends Well, Act 1, Scene 1 (the Countess)

text: How far that little candle throws his beams! So shines a good deed in a naughty world.
author: William Shakespeare
source: The Merchant of Venice, Act 5, Scene 1 (Portia)

text: Whoever lives by the guidance of reason strives, as far as possible, to repay another's hatred, anger and contempt with love, or generosity.
author: Baruch Spinoza

text: Hatred is increased by reciprocal hatred, and can on the contrary be destroyed by love.
author: Baruch Spinoza

text: There are no bonds holier than comradeship!
author: Nikolai Gogol

text: Leave me alone. Why do you hurt me?
author: Nikolai Gogol

text: Compassion is the chief and perhaps the only law of all human existence.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: “Well, brother,” he mumbled, “thanks for this too. This is also alms, brother.”
author: Ivan Turgenev

text: When partners can't agree, their work won't go well, and what comes of it is not work but only torment.
author: Ivan Krylov

text: Ah! I love those things that touch my heart and make me shed tears of tender sorrow!
author: Nikolai Karamzin

text: One old friend is better than two new ones.
author: Russian proverb

text: Good will not die, and evil will perish.
author: Russian proverb

text: My friends, how fair our union is! Like the soul, it is indivisible and eternal.
author: Alexander Pushkin

text: I loved you so sincerely, so tenderly, as God grant you may be loved by another.
author: Alexander Pushkin

text: We almost always forgive what we understand.
author: Mikhail Lermontov

text: Love hinders death. Love is life.
author: Leo Tolstoy

text: All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.
author: Leo Tolstoy

text: Love, I thought, is stronger than death and the fear of death. Only by it, only by love, does life hold together and move.
author: Ivan Turgenev

text: Let us be, first and foremost, kind, then honest, and then let us never forget one another.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: When a friend comes from far away, is that not a delight?
author: Confucius

text: What you do not want for yourself, do not do to others.
author: Confucius

text: One hand clapping alone, however fast, makes no sound.
author: Han Feizi
source: Han Feizi, ch. 28 «Achievement and Reputation» (Gong Ming)

text: The more you do for others, the more you have; the more you give to others, the richer you become.
author: Laozi

text: Answer resentment with kindness.
author: Laozi

text: Peach Blossom Pool is a thousand feet deep, yet not as deep as Wang Lun's friendship as he saw me off.
author: Li Bai

text: Care for your own elders and extend that care to the elders of others; love your own children and extend that love to the children of others.
author: Mencius

text: The feeling of compassion is the seed of humaneness.
author: Mencius

text: Those who love others are always loved by them; those who respect others are always respected.
author: Mencius

text: Whoever loves others will surely be loved in return; whoever does good to others will surely receive good in return.
author: Mozi
source: Mozi, ch. 15 «Universal Love II» (Jian Ai Zhong)

text: I only wish that we may all live long and, a thousand li apart, still share the beauty of the same moon.
author: Su Shi
source: To the tune Shui Diao Ge Tou (Mid-Autumn, 1076)

text: Once born into this world, we are all brothers and sisters; why must we be kin by blood?
author: Tao Yuanming

text: Fleabane growing among hemp stands straight without support. So choose carefully where you live, and keep the company of good people.
author: Xunzi

text: Those who rightly criticize me are my teachers; those who rightly approve of me are my friends; those who flatter me harm me.
author: Xunzi

text: Friendship between noble people is plain as water; between petty people, sweet as wine. The plain grows closer; the sweet breaks apart.
author: Zhuangzi

text: Staying too long in one place dulls a person's shine: go out into the world, and be renewed.
author: Abu Tammam
source: Poem 'Sarat tastajir al-dam' khawfa nawa ghad', verse beginning 'wa tul maqam al-mar''

text: Let go of what is past, and once you resolve, rely on what is real.
author: Antara ibn Shaddad
source: Poem 'Da' ma mada laka fi al-zaman al-awwal', v. 1

text: If you can do something today, do it.
author: Antara ibn Shaddad

author: Afanasy Fet

text: If life deceives you, do not grieve, do not be angry! On a day of gloom, accept it: a day of joy, believe me, will come.
author: Alexander Pushkin

text: No, life is not over at 31.
author: Leo Tolstoy

text: The music plays so cheerfully, so briskly, and you want to live!
author: Anton Chekhov

text: But I do not want to die, O friends; I want to live, to think and to suffer.
author: Alexander Pushkin

text: And it was worth living, and it was worth working.
author: Vladimir Mayakovsky

text: What matters is not fame, not glamour, not what I dreamed of, but the ability to endure.
author: Anton Chekhov

text: Only when the year turns cold do we see that the pine and cypress are the last to fade.
author: Confucius

text: A whirlwind does not last all morning; a sudden downpour does not last all day.
author: Laozi

text: Good fortune leans on misfortune; misfortune hides inside good fortune.
author: Laozi

text: Nothing is softer than water, yet nothing surpasses it in wearing down the hard. The weak overcomes the strong; the soft overcomes the rigid.
author: Laozi

text: Whenever your actions fail to succeed, turn and look for the cause in yourself.
author: Mencius

text: Before Heaven gives someone a great task, it first tries their resolve and tires their body, to toughen them and add to what they could not do.
author: Mencius

text: Life springs from worry and hardship; ruin comes from ease and comfort.
author: Mencius

text: Doing something is like digging a well: dig very deep but stop before reaching water, and it is still an abandoned well.
author: Mencius

text: The past cannot be mended, but the future can still be pursued. I have not strayed far: today I see what was wrong yesterday.
author: Tao Yuanming

text: You must be tempered in real affairs; only then can you stand firm, steady in stillness and steady in action.
author: Wang Yangming
source: Instructions for Practical Living (Chuanxi Lu), vol. 1, §23

text: A thoroughbred cannot cover ten paces in one leap; a slow horse goes far in ten days, because it does not give up.
author: Xunzi

text: Carve and then quit, and not even rotten wood will break; carve and never quit, and even metal and stone can be engraved.
author: Xunzi

text: Step by step without resting, even a lame turtle can go a thousand li.
author: Xunzi

text: So much effort once wasted trying to push it; today the ship sails freely in midstream.
author: Zhu Xi
source: Thoughts on Reading, No. 2 (Guan Shu You Gan)
